links.note: 361 calls craving (அவா) the seed (வித்து) that yields unfailing birth (தவாஅப் பிறப்பு ஈனும்) for all beings at all times. 349 says the moment attachment ends it cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). The two state one causal claim from both ends: craving produces birth, and its ending stops birth.

361 uses வித்து for craving, the seed from which birth keeps growing. 24 uses the same word for the person who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness: he is a seed for the ground called வரன் (வரனென்னும் வைப்பிற்கோர் வித்து), which Parimelazhagar takes as the ground of release. The seed figure is used for both outcomes, rebirth from craving and release from restraint of the senses.

362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not-wanting (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக ... பற்று விடற்கு). Both turn the fault against itself: wanting and clinging are given a single object whose effect is to end them.

265 says austerity is pursued here because whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 362 narrows what is worth wanting to one thing, not being born (வேண்டுங்கால் வேண்டும் பிறவாமை), and says it is reached by wanting not to want. Read together, 362 limits the open promise of 265 to a single proper wish.

180, on not coveting others' goods, says the pride called not-wanting yields victory (விறல்ஈனும் வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு); Parimelazhagar glosses செருக்கு there as wealth. 363 says there is no fine wealth like not-wanting (வேண்டாமை அன்ன விழுச்செல்வம்) here or there. The householder's restraint toward another's property becomes, in the renouncer's chapter, not wanting anything at all, and in both it is counted as a possession.

363 says nothing here (ஈண்டு) or there (ஆண்டும்) equals not-wanting. 213 says that in the world of the gods and here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing what is due to others. The same two-world formula ranks a different thing highest in each setting: giving to the world in the householder's book, wanting nothing in the renouncer's.

Both verses use விழுச்செல்வம், fine wealth, for something that is not goods. 400 says learning is the imperishable fine wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை); 363 says no fine wealth is like not-wanting. The pairing shows the book repeatedly moving the word wealth away from property, to learning in one place and to the absence of want in another.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 364 says purity is the absence of craving (தூஉய்மை என்பது அவாவின்மை) and that this comes by wanting வாய்மை. 364 puts a step between the two terms of 298: truth leads to freedom from craving, and that is what purity is. Manakkudavar reads வாய்மை in 364 as truthful speech, as in 298; Parimelazhagar reads it as the true reality.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 364 defines purity as the absence of craving (அவாவின்மை). Taken together, 364 names the stain that 34 leaves unnamed.

365 says those called freed (அற்றவர்) are those freed of craving, and the rest (மற்றையார்) are not freed in that way. 348 says those who have renounced completely (தீரத் துறந்தார்) have arrived, and the rest (மற்றையவர்) are confused and caught in the net. Both divide people into two groups with no middle, and both make completeness the test.

275 warns that the hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' (பற்றற்றேம் என்பார்) brings many harms. 365 says who may rightly be called freed (அற்றவர் என்பார்): only those freed of craving. 275 shows the claim made falsely; 365 gives the inner criterion that the claim has to meet.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, one of which is craving (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 366 says craving is what deceives a person (வஞ்சிப்பது அவா), and that fearing it is itself virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). 366 takes one item from the list in 35 and gives the reason for singling it out: it works by deceit, so it needs constant watch.

428 says fearing what should be feared is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்) and leaves the object open. 366 names an object, craving, and calls the fear of it virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). The general rule about right fear in the book of statecraft gets a specific content in the renouncer's chapter.

Fear and craving appear together in both verses with opposite roles. In 1075 fear is the whole conduct of the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), with a little more if there is something they crave (அவாவுண்டேல்); Parimelazhagar takes the fear as fear of punishment. In 366 fear is directed at craving itself and is called virtue. The pairing separates fear that serves craving from fear that guards against it.

266 says those who do austerity do their own work, and the others, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, the deed that does not fail (தவாவினை) comes in the way one wishes. They state the same link from opposite sides: desire makes action futile, and its removal makes action unfailing.

309 says all that one has thought of is reached at once if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 367 says the unfailing deed comes as one wishes (தான் வேண்டுமாற்றான் வரும்) once craving is cut. Each verse removes one passion, anger or craving, and promises that what one intends then arrives.

341 says a person has no pain from each thing he has left (யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் அதனின் இலன்), taking objects one by one. 368 says those without craving have no sorrow at all (அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம்). 368 moves from the objects given up to the craving behind them, so the relief is complete instead of item by item.

347 says sorrows hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள்). 368 says that where craving exists sorrow keeps coming without fail, one after another (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்). Both describe suffering as continuing for as long as its cause is kept.

628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow. The renouncer's doctrine reappears as practical advice for a person at work in the world, where Parimelazhagar relates it to the pains of effort.

The two verses share one sentence frame. 369: joy is unbroken if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes (அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). 854: it yields the joy of joys if the sorrow of sorrows called hostility perishes (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). The same title, sorrow of sorrows, is given to craving in the book of virtue and to hostility in the book of statecraft, each as the worst thing in its own field.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா). 940 gives a picture of that: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), a living being's love grows with each suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar takes this as love of the body. 940 shows why satisfying craving cannot end it, which is why 370 says it has to be given up.

370 says that giving up craving gives, in that very state (அந்நிலையே), a nature that does not shift (பேரா இயற்கை). 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) it cuts off birth. Both make the result immediate on the cause ending, with no further step between.

371 says tireless effort arises from a fate of gain and sloth arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 618 says lacking good fortune (பொறியின்மை) is no one's disgrace, but lacking effort after learning what should be known is a disgrace (ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). If sloth itself is produced by fate, as 371 says on a plain reading, the line 618 draws between blameless fortune and blameworthy idleness is hard to hold.

594 says prosperity asks the way and goes to the one whose energy does not flag (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான்). 371 uses the same word, அசைவின்மை, and says it arises from a fate of gain (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும்). 594 presents unflagging energy as what draws fortune; 371 puts a favourable fate behind that energy.

617 says the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி) and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the one without sloth. 371 says sloth (மடி) and its opposite are themselves produced by the fate of loss and the fate of gain. In 617 fortune depends on whether one is slothful; 371 adds that whether one is slothful depends on fate.

372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை). 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால்), and to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel at it. In both, approaching gain or ruin shows first as a change in the person's own judgement.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ்); Parimelazhagar adds that this happens even to one who has understanding. The protection 429 promises rests on understanding, and 372 says understanding itself can be taken away by fate.

396 says understanding wells up in people to the extent they have learned (கற்றனைத்து ஊறும் அறிவு), like water in a sand well. 373 says that however many subtle books a person studies, the understanding that is truly his own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). On the reading that உண்மையறிவு is a fixed native understanding, which Parimelazhagar ties to fate, study does not decide how much a person understands, and the two conflict. Parimelazhagar notes the conflict himself under 396 and resolves it by saying 396 holds where fate does not oppose.

373 separates understanding gained from books (நூல்பல கற்பினும்) from a person's own understanding (தன் உண்மையறிவு) and says the second prevails. 636 names the same pair, natural acuteness together with books (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு), and says no subtle scheme can stand before a minister who has both. 373 ranks the two; 636 shows the best case, where both are present.

823 says that even after learning many good things it is hard for the unworthy to become good in heart (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது); Parimelazhagar applies this to enemies. 373 says that after much study a person's own understanding still prevails. The same limit on what books can change is stated once for understanding and once for the heart.

374 says the world's nature is of two separate kinds: being wealthy is one thing and being clear-minded is another (திருவேறு தெள்ளியராதலும் வேறு). 430 says those with understanding have everything (அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார்). If 'everything' in 430 includes wealth, as Parimelazhagar explains it by saying wealth is made and kept by understanding, the two conflict; under 374 he says the opposite, that understanding is not even a contributing cause of wealth. If 430 only means that understanding outweighs possessions, there is no conflict.

374 states as a general fact that wealth and clear understanding are separate lots. 408 judges one result of that: wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 408 takes for granted the mismatch that 374 explains.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and gives no answer; Parimelazhagar says the wise look for the earlier deed behind it. 374 notes a like mismatch between wealth and understanding and gives it as the two-fold nature of the world. One verse separates wealth from goodness and the other separates it from wisdom.

483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the right means and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 375 says that in making wealth all that is good turns bad and bad turns good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம்); Parimelazhagar takes the good and bad things to be time, place, means and action, reversed by fate. On that reading the favourable conditions 483 relies on do not secure the result, and the two conflict. Kalaignar reads 375 differently, as good and bad deeds turning out contrary to intent.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however carefully it is guarded (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if thrown out. 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, and what is of the good kind (நற்பாலவை) pays later even if lost. Both say some goods stay and some go whatever one does; 659 gives a test the person controls, the way the wealth was gained, where 376 gives only fate's allotment.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்), and treats this as the miser's own failing. 377 says even those who have gathered crores can enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). Both separate owning from enjoying; 377 places part of enjoyment outside the owner's choice, which limits the blame in 1005.

385 lists the king's skills with wealth: creating, gathering, guarding and apportioning what is guarded (காத்த வகுத்தலும்). 377 uses the same verb for the one who apportions each person's enjoyment (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை), whom Parimelazhagar glosses as தெய்வம். The pairing sets the human apportioner of the state's wealth beside the apportioner who decides what even the gatherer of crores may enjoy.

377 and 1062 are two places where the book puts a personal agent behind people's lots: the apportioner (வகுத்தான்) in 377 and the one who made the world (உலகியற்றியான்) in 1062. 377 states his allotment as a fact that limits enjoyment. 1062 says that if he meant some to live even by begging, may he wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக). One verse accepts the allotment and the other curses its author for one kind of lot.

Both verses begin with the same people, those without means of enjoyment (துப்புரவு இல்லார்), and both speak of their renouncing. 1050 says that their not renouncing fully (துவரத் துறவாமை) makes them death to others' salt and gruel. 378 says they would renounce if what they are due to undergo passed without afflicting them (உறற்பால ஊட்டா கழியுமெனின்). 378 gives the reason for the failure 1050 complains of: fate still makes them live through what is due. Kalaignar reads 378 differently, as renouncing when troubling feelings fall away.

344 says having nothing is natural to austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை). 378 looks at those who already have nothing through poverty and says they would renounce, but for what fate makes them undergo. Parimelazhagar makes the connection: they have already lost what a renouncer gives up, and still suffer because their intent differs. Having nothing is the condition of austerity in 344, and 378 shows it is not enough by itself.

379 asks why those who see things as good when good comes should grieve (அல்லற்படுவது எவன்) when it does not. 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve (அல்லற்படுபவோ) saying 'we have lost it'. Both are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry between gain and loss. 626 adds the practical point that grief at loss depends on how one held the gain.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. 379 asks why one who accepts the good should grieve at its opposite. Both ask for the same response to both turns of fortune, and Parimelazhagar refers both verses to the results of earlier deeds.

629 says one who does not desire the pleasure within pleasure does not suffer the pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 379 asks why people who take the good as good (நல்லவாக் காண்பவர்) suffer when the bad comes. 629 supplies an answer to that question: the suffering follows from the relish, and ends with it.

380 asks what is stronger than fate, since even when one devises another course it gets there first (மற்றொன்று சூழினுந் தான்முந்துறும்). 620 says those who labour on without flagging or delay will see even fate's back (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). On a plain reading 620 says effort can defeat fate and 380 says nothing can, so they conflict. Parimelazhagar softens 620 to mean that fate cannot be averted in one or two attempts, so those who try repeatedly reach the result.

Both verses end with the same phrase, தான் முந்துறும். In 380 it is fate that gets ahead of whatever a person plans against it. In 1023 it is தெய்வம் that tucks up its garment and goes ahead of the one who says 'I will raise my family' (குடிசெய்வல்). The same power that outruns human planning in the chapter on fate is shown going in front of human resolve in the chapter on raising one's family.

380 says fate is the strongest thing and gets ahead of any plan. 619 grants that a thing may not come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), and adds that effort still pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 619 accepts the limit that 380 states and marks out what remains for effort within it.
